article.title: I Miss You in Sinhala: Four Forms, Checked Against a Dictionary
article.excerpt: "I miss you" in Sinhala is මට ඔයාව මතක් වෙනවා — Carter's 1924 dictionary glosses that verb "to occur to one's mind, remember". Sinhala has no verb for missing a person: all four entries for "miss" are about hitting a target. Four forms, who each is for, and the prefix that reverses it.

faqs.question: How do you say I miss you in Sinhala?
faqs.answer: The everyday line is මට ඔයාව මතක් වෙනවා (maṭa oyāwa matak wenawā). Carter's 1924 Sinhalese-English dictionary glosses the verb මතක්වෙනවා at page 472 as "to occur to one's mind, remember", so it literally says you come to my mind. Sinhala has no single verb that means missing a person.

faqs.question: Does මට ඔයාව මතක් වෙනවා really mean I miss you, or does it mean I remember you?
faqs.answer: Strictly, it means the second. The dictionary gloss is "to occur to one's mind, remember". In everyday use it is what a Sri Lankan sends when an English speaker would send "I miss you", so it is the right line — but it is an approximation, not an equivalent, and it is honest to know that.

faqs.question: What is the difference between මතක and අමතක?
faqs.answer: One prefix, and it reverses the meaning. Carter has මතක at page 472 as "remembrance, recollection" and අ·මතකය at page 54 as "forgetting, forgetfulness, oblivion" — the privative අ- in front of the same root. A line built on අමතක is about forgetting, not missing.

faqs.question: Is there a Sinhala phrase that actually carries the ache?
faqs.answer: ඔයා නැතුව මට පාළුයි (oyā nätuwa maṭa pāḷuyi), roughly "without you I'm desolate". Carter glosses පාළු at page 380 as "vacant, uncultivated, waste, desolate, desert" — the word Sinhala uses for abandoned land. Send it to a partner, not to a colleague.

faqs.question: Should I use ඔයා or ඔබ?
faqs.answer: ඔයා for a friend, a sibling or a partner your own age; ඔබ for anyone older or senior and for anything written. English Wiktionary labels ඔයා informal and ඔබ formal. Never use තෝ, which Wiktionary labels derogatory.

faqs.question: Can I just use the English word miss inside a Sinhala sentence?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is normal rather than lazy. මට ඔයාව මිස් වෙනවා is a standard insertion. A 2021 study of 30 urban Sinhala-English bilinguals found insertion to be the dominant code-mixing strategy and the mixed variety to be the preferred code for neutralising attitude — which is exactly what you want when the native word feels too heavy.

faqs.question: Should I write it in Sinhala script or in English letters?
faqs.answer: Romanised for a person, script for anything a machine has to handle. A 2026 benchmark of 24 language models on Sinhala reports Unicode in formal contexts and romanised text dominating social media, with median performance degradation exceeding 300 times from Unicode to romanised text.

faqs.question: How do I pronounce mata oyawa matak wenawa?
faqs.answer: Roughly MA-ta O-ya-wa ma-TAK we-na-WA, with the a in each syllable short. The romanisation used here follows Carter's own transliteration (mataka, pāḷu, oba, matakvenavā), where ā is a long a and ḷ is a retroflex l.

faqs.question: Will a Sri Lankan Tamil understand any of these lines?
faqs.answer: No. Sri Lanka has two official languages: Sinhala is Indo-Aryan, Tamil is Dravidian, and none of these four forms transfers. Sending a Sinhala line to a Sri Lankan Tamil is a visible mistake rather than a near miss, so ask if you are not sure.

faqs.question: How much should I write around the Sinhala line?
faqs.answer: Less than you think. Across 214 miss-you pages on SubhSandesh the median letter is 88 words and the longest is 1,024, so one translated line plus two or three sentences of your own is already a normal-length letter.

faqs.question: Can I send a Sinhala line with a photo, a voice note and a countdown around it?
faqs.answer: Yes — that is what the miss-you page template at subhsandesh.in/missyou-gf is for, and the voice note is the one place the pronunciation actually survives. Only 13.6% of senders record one, 29 of 214, which is why it still reads as effort. Note the page's own labels and buttons are in English, so your Sinhala line sits inside an English frame.

faqs.question: Can I keep a Sinhala miss-you page private?
faqs.answer: You can password-protect it before sharing, and this is the segment where people most often do: 43.5% of miss-you senders, 93 of 214, against 38.5% across the whole platform. The database records which template was opened, never who received it.

article.contentMarkdown:
# I Miss You in Sinhala: Four Forms, Checked Against a Dictionary

Sinhala has no single verb meaning "to miss a person". Search Charles Carter's [*A Sinhalese-English Dictionary*](https://dsal.uchicago.edu/cgi-bin/app/carter_query.py?qs=miss&matchtype=exact) (Colombo, 1924) for "miss" and four entries come back — නොවැදීයාම "failing to strike", වරද්දනවා "to err, miss", වාරාවෙනවා "to miss the mark or aim", මුක්තකය, a missile. Every one is about failing to hit something.

The everyday line is **මට ඔයාව මතක් වෙනවා** (*maṭa oyāwa matak wenawā*), and Carter glosses මතක්වෙනවා at page 472 as "to occur to one's mind, remember" — not "to miss". The page around the line carries more than the words do: across 214 "I miss you" pages built on /missyou-gf since 2026-07-28, 43.5% of senders password-protect the page before sharing, against 38.5% platform-wide, and the median letter is 88 words.

## The prefix that reverses the sentence

Sinhala negates with a prefix, and it costs one syllable. Carter lists අ·මතකය at page 54 as "forgetting, forgetfulness, oblivion" — that is මතක, "remembrance, recollection" (page 472), with the privative අ- in front of it.

This is not a theoretical hazard. One of the pages currently ranking for this query offers මම ඔයාට හුගාක් අමතකයි as "the most common way to say I miss you in Sinhala" and glosses අමතකයි as "remember". It is built on the word for forgetting.

The other confusion is ආදරය — Carter page 90, "love, affection, regard", traced by English Wiktionary to Sanskrit आदर. A line built on ආදරය says *I love you*. That is a different message, and to a colleague who has moved countries it is the wrong one.

## The four forms, and what each one actually says

### 1. මට ඔයාව මතක් වෙනවා — maṭa oyāwa matak wenawā

The default spoken line, and the closest thing to a neutral "I miss you". It is built on the dative: මට is "to me", and the verb happens *to* you rather than being done *by* you. The Tatoeba corpus attests exactly this frame in [sentence 2968421](https://tatoeba.org/en/sentences/show/2968421), මට ඔබ ඇහෙනවා, translated "I hear you".

Literally it says *you come to my mind*. That is gentler than English "I miss you" and it is what most Sri Lankans would text a friend, a sibling or a parent.

### 2. ඔයා නැතුව මට පාළුයි — oyā nätuwa maṭa pāḷuyi

This is the one that carries the ache. Carter lists පාළු at page 380 as "vacant, uncultivated, waste, desolate, desert", and පාළුව as "waste or desolate place or state". නැති at page 323 is "which is or are not".

So the sentence reads, word by word, *without you, to me, desolate*. The word you reach for to say you are lonely is the word Sinhala uses for abandoned land. Send it to a partner or to someone you are genuinely raw about; it is too heavy for a colleague.

One spelling note: Carter's headword uses the retroflex ළ, පාළු, while the form circulating online is usually written පාලු. Both are read the same way.

### 3. මට ඔයාව මිස් වෙනවා — maṭa oyāwa mis wenawā

The English word, dropped into the Sinhala frame. This is not lazy and it is not wrong. Shashikala's 2021 study of 30 urban Sinhala-English bilinguals in the [*Open Journal of Modern Linguistics*](https://www.scirp.org/journal/paperinformation?paperid=108322) found insertion to be the dominant code-mixing strategy in their speech, and that the mixed variety is the preferred code for neutralising attitude.

Neutralising attitude is precisely the job here. මිස් lets you say it without committing to the weight of පාළු. Sinhala is absent from all 69 languages in Wiktionary's ["I miss you" phrasebook entry](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/I_miss_you), but Bengali is there with both routes side by side: আমার তোমাকে মনে পড়ছে natively, and আমি তোমাকে মিস করছি marked colloquial.

### 4. ඔබව මතක් වෙනවා — obawa matak wenawā

The same verb with the formal pronoun — for an older relative, a teacher, or anyone you address respectfully. It is also the form that survives into writing.

## How the four compare

| Form | Glossed in Carter 1924 as | Who it suits | Where it goes on a miss-you page |
|---|---|---|---|
| මට ඔයාව මතක් වෙනවා | "to occur to one's mind, remember" (p. 472) | friend, sibling, parent | the letter — median length 88 words across 214 pages |
| ඔයා නැතුව මට පාළුයි | "vacant, waste, desolate, desert" (p. 380) | partner, someone you are raw about | the voice note — only 13.6% of senders, 29 of 214, record one |
| මට ඔයාව මිස් වෙනවා | not in Carter; English insertion | anyone, when you want it light | the page headline, where a mixed line reads naturally |
| ඔබව මතක් වෙනවා | ඔබ is "pron. hon. thou" (p. 140) | elders, teachers, anyone senior | the "open when" letters — 92.1% of pages carry at least one |

## Who you are allowed to say it to

Sinhala makes you choose a second person before you can say anything at all, and the choice is not neutral. English Wiktionary marks [ඔයා](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E0%B6%94%E0%B6%BA%E0%B7%8F) as informal "you" with ඔබ as its formal synonym; තෝ is marked derogatory, inherited from Sanskrit त्व; නුඹ is marked honorific.

Carter, a century earlier, has ඔබ at page 140 as "pron. hon. thou" and නුඹ at page 339 as plain "thou, you". ඔයා — the one you would actually text — is not in Carter at all.

Two practical rules follow. Use ඔයා for a friend, a sibling or a partner your own age. Use ඔබ for anyone older or senior, and for anything written. Never use තෝ, in any register, to anyone you are missing.

## Spoken and written Sinhala are two registers, not one

Of the six pages on the current result set for this query that I could fetch, none mentions the spoken/written split at all. It is the part that will trip you up: the form you text is not the form you would write on a formal card.

The corpus shows the spoken side plainly. Tatoeba sentence 13213063, මම වතුර බොනවා, is "I drink water"; sentence 13213137, ටොම් වතුර බොනවා, is "Tom drinks water". Same verb form, බොනවා, for "I" and for "Tom" — spoken Sinhala does not mark the subject on the verb. The literary register does, which is why the two look like different languages on the page.

The honest limit: the standard academic treatment, James Gair's "Sinhala Diglossia Revisited, or Diglossia Dies Hard" (Oxford University Press, 1998), sits behind a paywall, so the claim here rests on the corpus evidence above rather than on that chapter.

## Sinhala script or romanised — and why it changes what arrives

Sri Lankans write Sinhala two ways, and the search results that translate this phrase almost all assume the first one. A 2026 benchmark of 24 open-source language models on [Unicode, romanised and mixed-script Sinhala](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.14958) reports that "Unicode [is] used in formal contexts and Romanized text dominating social media", and measures median performance degradation exceeding 300 times from Unicode to romanised text.

The consequence is blunt. *Mata oyawa matak wenawa* in Latin letters reads instantly to a Sri Lankan and badly to every machine in between. මට ඔයාව මතක් වෙනවා in script looks more formal, and translation tools handle it far better.

Pick by reader, not by tool: romanised is warmer to a person, script survives a copy-paste.

## Sinhala is not Sri Lankan Tamil

Sri Lanka has two official languages. Sinhala is Indo-Aryan, Tamil is Dravidian, and nothing in this post transfers. If the person you are writing to is a Sri Lankan Tamil, none of these four lines is theirs, and sending one is a visible mistake rather than a near miss.

If you are not sure, ask — a shorter conversation than the one that follows getting it wrong.

## What 214 miss-you pages show about the letter around the line

These numbers come from two read-only probes of our own database on 2026-09-25, covering 214 pages built on /missyou-gf since the template went live on 2026-07-28. That is two months of data at n = 214, so nothing seasonal can be read out of it.

Recipients tapped "hug" 1,434 times across 138 of those 214 pages, 64.5% receiving at least one and 512 on a single page. 2,417 views were recorded, 11.3 per page — though views count page opens, not unique visitors, so one recipient reopening a page twenty times is twenty views.

The letter is short: median 88 words, longest 1,024. A translated line plus two sentences of your own is already normal length here, which helps if you feared one Sinhala sentence would look thin.

What the database does not record is who received anything. It records which template was opened, never the recipient — so none of these figures describes a Sri Lankan audience specifically, and no claim here should be read that way.

## When our page is the wrong place for a Sinhala line

The [miss-you page for a partner](https://subhsandesh.in/missyou-gf) is the template built for exactly this message, and it is the one to reach for if you want the line to arrive with a photo, a countdown and a voice note around it. 28.0% of senders set a reunion date; 60 of 214.

It half-works for a Sinhala sender, and it is worth saying which half. The furniture — the labels, the prompts, the button text — is English. Your Sinhala line sits inside an English frame, which is fine for a bilingual recipient and slightly odd for a monolingual one. The city field is a picker with a default, so the 47 city pairs recorded across those pages are not evidence of what senders chose to say.

If the Sinhala line is the whole point and you want it revealed slowly rather than displayed, [The Last Piece photo puzzle](https://subhsandesh.in/photo-puzzle) suits that reader better: each piece placed uncovers one line of the letter, so the romanised line and its meaning can land separately instead of competing in the same block of text. For everything else, [browse the full set of templates](https://subhsandesh.in/templates).

And if you want the comparison across languages rather than the depth in one, the [I miss you in different languages](https://subhsandesh.in/blog/i-miss-you-in-different-languages) hub is the page for that.

## Sources

- Carter, Charles. *A Sinhalese-English Dictionary*. Colombo: "Ceylon Observer" Printing Works; London: Probsthain & Co., 1924. Served by the Digital Dictionaries of South Asia.
- English Wiktionary, Sinhala entries and the "I miss you" phrasebook translation table.
- Tatoeba, Sinhala sentence set.
- Rajapakse & Weerasinghe, "Script Sensitivity: Benchmarking Language Models on Unicode, Romanized and Mixed-Script Sinhala", arXiv, 2026.
- Shashikala, H. "Exploring the Sociolinguistic Aspects of Sinhala-English Code-Mixing among Urban Sri Lankan Bilingual Speakers". *Open Journal of Modern Linguistics* 11, 2021.

English Wiktionary's "I miss you" phrasebook entry lists translations into 69 top-level languages. Sinhala is not one of them. Bengali carries both routes side by side — আমার তোমাকে মনে পড়ছে (ami tōmake mone poṛche) natively and আমি তোমাকে মিস করছি (ami tōmake mis korchi) marked colloquial — and Hindi and Urdu both build the phrase on याद / یاد, "memory".

English Wiktionary's Sinhala pronoun entries (the language header there is "Sinhalese"): ඔයා is labelled informal "you", with ඔබ given as its formal synonym; ඔබ is labelled formal "you"; තෝ is labelled derogatory "you, thou", inherited from Sanskrit त्व; නුඹ is labelled honorific "you". ආදරය is a borrowing from Sanskrit आदर glossed "love" then "respect". මතක is glossed "remembrance, recollection", referenced to Carter page 472.

The Tatoeba Sinhala sentence set contains 75 sentences in total, and not one of them contains මතක, පාළු, අඩු, මිස්, සිහි or any other form of missing or remembering a person. Sentence 2968421, මට ඔබ ඇහෙනවා, is translated "I hear you" and attests the dative-experiencer frame මට + [you] + verb. Sentences 13213063 (මම වතුර බොනවා, "I drink water") and 13213137 (ටොම් වතුර බොනවා, "Tom drinks water") carry the identical verb form බොනවා for a first-person and a third-person subject, showing that the spoken register does not mark the subject on the verb.

Rajapakse and Weerasinghe, "Script Sensitivity: Benchmarking Language Models on Unicode, Romanized and Mixed-Script Sinhala" (arXiv preprint, submitted 2026-01-21). The abstract states that "Sinhala exhibits script duality, with Unicode used in formal contexts and Romanized text dominating social media, while mixed-script usage is common in practice", and reports across 24 open-source language models "median performance degradation exceeding 300 times from Unicode to Romanized text". Abstract read; the PDF was not parsed.

Shashikala, H. (2021), "Exploring the Sociolinguistic Aspects of Sinhala-English Code-Mixing among Urban Sri Lankan Bilingual Speakers", Open Journal of Modern Linguistics 11, 158-173, doi:10.4236/ojml.2021.112014 (open access, verified via Unpaywall). Sample of 30 employed bilinguals in Sri Lanka's main urban city. Findings: the mixed variety "is undoubtedly the preferred code for expressing neutralization of attitudes in speech", and structurally "insertion" is the major code-mixing strategy while congruent lexicalization is the least used. Full HTML text read.

structuralLimitations: BRIEF CORRECTION. BRIEF.md section 3 says "Sinhala — Clough". DSAL does not serve Clough: https://dsal.uchicago.edu/dictionaries/clough/ returns 404, and the Sinhala dictionary DSAL actually serves is Charles Carter, A Sinhalese-English Dictionary (Colombo, 1924), at https://dsal.uchicago.edu/dictionaries/carter/ with a working carter_query.py endpoint. Clough 1892 exists only as scans on archive.org (identifier sinhaleseenglish00clourich), whose Sinhala-script OCR is unreliable. Every dictionary claim in this post is from Carter, with page numbers, and English Wiktionary's Sinhala entries reference the same dictionary (R:si:Carter), so the two instruments agree.

TASK-PROMPT CORRECTION. The prompt named "මට ඔයාව මතකයි / මං ඔයාට ආදරෙයි" as "the standard rendering". They are not two renderings of one thing and the second is not a miss-you line at all: ආදරය is Carter page 90, "love, affection, regard". Neither string is used in this post. The post uses the attested spoken forms instead.

en.wiktionary.org uses the L2 header "Sinhalese", not "Sinhala", which is why a naive section lookup returns nothing. Coverage is thin: මතක, ඔයා, ඔබ, ආදරය, මම, තෝ and නුඹ have entries; මතක්, නැති, මිස්, සිහි, අඩු, මතකය, ඔයාව and අමතක all 404.

Sinhala diglossia has a standard academic treatment — James Gair, "Sinhala Diglossia Revisited, or Diglossia Dies Hard", Studies in South Asian Linguistics, OUP 1998, doi:10.1093/oso/9780195095210.003.0017 — and Unpaywall reports it is not open access, with no OA location. The register claim in this post therefore rests on a corpus minimal pair (Tatoeba 13213063 vs 13213137) and on Carter's own inventory, not on Gair. Re-check if the chapter is ever deposited.

The arXiv script-sensitivity paper is a preprint, not peer-reviewed, and only its abstract was read; the PDF was not parsed. Both numbers cited (script duality, >300x median degradation) are stated in the abstract itself.

Lines considered and cut: (a) මම ඔයාට හුගාක් අමතකයි, offered as the standard translation by the page ranking first on this SERP — cut because Carter page 54 gives අ·මතකය as "forgetting, forgetfulness, oblivion"; it appears in the post only as the error it is. (b) මට ඔයාගේ අඩුව දැනෙනවා, "I feel your lack" — cut because Carter has අඩු (p. 15, "deficient; less, lower; low") and දැනෙනවා (p. 283) as headwords but not the compound අඩුව, so the full phrase could not be verified against the instrument. (c) A literary-register verb form such as -මි for the first person — cut because no attested literary sentence for this meaning could be fetched, so the post states that the written register marks person without printing an unverified example.

Spelling variant recorded rather than silently normalised: Carter's headword is පාළු with retroflex ළ; the form circulating in translation memories and forum answers is usually written පාලු with ල. The post uses the dictionary spelling and names the variant.

SERP measurement. The eight results in SERPS-WAVE2.md were attempted; six returned content (talkpal.ai, indifferentlanguages.com, linguashop.com, mymemory.translated.net, answers.com, italki.com), howtosayguide.com refused the connection, and translate.google.com is a tool, not a page. Of the six fetched, zero mention diglossia, colloquial-versus-literary register, or a spoken/written split, and only one references any dictionary. That is the measured basis for the claim in the register section; it is not a claim about pages I did not fetch.

No table column can be built from first-party message language: the /missyou-gf probes record letter length, password use, hug taps, reunion dates and voice notes, but nothing segmentable by which language a sender wrote in. The table's fourth column therefore maps each form to a page surface using platform-wide figures, not Sinhala-specific ones. Re-check if a language or script field is ever added to the letter and n passes ~500.

auditReport.honestAssessment: An answer engine would cite this over the pages analysed because it is the only one that went to a named dictionary and reported what it found: Carter 1924 returns four entries for "miss" and all four are about hitting a target, the everyday line is glossed "to remember", and the phrase the top-ranking page offers is built on the word for forgetting. Those are checkable claims with page numbers, which none of the six pages I fetched carries. The weaknesses are real: the SERP is weak but the domains on it are language-learning sites with far more topical authority for this query than a gifting site, the post is a translation spoke rather than a language resource, and no first-party number here is Sinhala-specific — the 214-page segment records no message language, so the platform data describes the envelope, not the Sinhala inside it. Ranking will take months if it happens at all.
